title: Before that
description: Say what had already happened before something else.
grammarNote: The pluperfect is the imperfect of haber plus the participle: había hablado, habías comido.

explanation.summary: The pluperfect is the past of the past. It says what had already happened before another past event, and it is how Spanish handles a sequence of past events.

sections.heading: How it is built
sections.body: The imperfect of haber, which is the same for every verb: había, habías, había, habíamos, habíais, habían, followed by the participle. The participles are the same ones you already know: hablado, comido, vivido, visto, hecho, escrito.

examples.en: When I arrived, they had already left.

examples.es: No comí porque no había preparado la comida.
examples.en: I did not eat because I had not prepared the food.
I had seen the film before.

sections.heading: Two pasts in a row
sections.body: The event that came first takes the pluperfect, and the one after it takes the preterite. Cuando llegué, ya habían salido: the leaving is earlier, so it is a pluperfect, and the arriving is the later event, so it is a preterite.

examples.es: Cuando terminé, ya me habían llamado.
examples.en: When I finished, they had already called me.

sections.heading: Almost never on its own
sections.body: You will not say the pluperfect alone very often. It earns its place when one past event explains another, or when someone reports something that had already happened.

examples.es: Cuando llegué a casa, ya había cenado.
examples.en: When I got home, I had already eaten.

examples.es: Supuso que yo había sido capaz.
examples.en: He assumed I had been able.

items.note: The pluperfect of ver. Visto is irregular.
The pluperfect of hacer. Hecho is irregular.
The pluperfect of decir. Dicho is irregular.
The pluperfect of escribir. Escrito is irregular.

drills.note: The pluperfect explains the other past event.

A report of a past event can carry the pluperfect.
